newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Election aftermath to overshadow NZ inflation data.
newsitem.headline: Election aftermath to overshadow NZ inflation data.

text.p: New Zealand inflation data due next week is likely to be eclipsed in the wake of a general election three days before, economists said on Wednesday.
They said the figures, due on Tuesday and expected to show underlying inflation well above the Reserve Bank's zero to two percent target, would cause little stir in financial markets.
Fourteen economists polled by Reuters expect on average an annual rise in underlying inflation of 2.6 percent, while the Reserve Bank itself has forecast a 2.7 percent annual rise.
Economists said the breach of the target band's ceiling was well flagged. As the RBNZ had a good record of picking inflation a quarter ahead, the data was unlikely to surprise.
Westpac economist Joselyn Stroombergen said the CPI would not get the attention it deserved.

"It's going to be completely overshadowed by the election and the horse-trading that will happen in the couple of days after it. People will be less interested, because they will be focusing on...who's doing deals with whom after the election."
New Zealanders go to the polls on Saturday for the country's first general election under a proportional voting system that favours minority or coalition governments.

Latest polls suggest a left-wing coalition of the main opposition Labour Party and either economic nationalist New Zealand First or the left-wing Alliance, or both, could oust the ruling conservative National Party.
Bankers Trust chief economist David Plank said a centre-left coalition with Labour at the helm, while not the preferred outcome, was something the markets could live with.

"As long as we get a fairly clear centre-right or centre-left victory, then the market on the Monday has a bit of a reaction but nothing too dramatic, and then the focus gets back onto the economics," he said.
"Where it might be nasty is if we get an unclear result on Saturday night...then it may overshadow the CPI."
Stroombergen said the December quarter CPI would hold more interest for markets, as it would reveal whether inflation peaked in the September quarter as the RBNZ predicted.

"That's the real crunch. Everyone is expecting this quarter to be a big one...it's just whether or not the next one actually shows the fall that everybody's looking for. The RB has made it pretty clear that until they see that fall, they're not going to ease," she said.
Bain and Co chief economist Ulf Schoefisch said tentative steps toward a market-led easing could be seen before year-end.

"If, after the election, circumstances are different, like a wider (RBNZ) target range emerges, I would think that if the markets take conditions lower the bank would allow that to happen, within limits obviously," he said. Labour proposes widening the inflation band to minus one to three percent.

Plank agreed the market could probably lead a slight easing without alarming the bank. However, an official easing could be delayed if the election produced a Labour-led coalition, as Labour's policies involved higher government spending.
"It may be that the Reserve Bank concludes that the fiscal easing does not allow it to ease monetary policy even with a slightly wider (target) band," Plank said.
